slides.title: Mobius Transformations
slides.notes: This opening frames Mobius transformations as geometry rather than as a bag of rational formulas. The main move is to enlarge the complex plane by one point so that poles and infinity become ordinary destinations of the same map. The lecture will repeatedly test algebraic claims against visible invariants.

slides.title: Route Through The Appendix
slides.notes: The sequence of topics is chosen to keep the geometry visible. Each new algebraic expression is paired with a geometric test: where infinity goes, whether a Circle stays a Circle, whether four-point data remains unchanged, and whether orientation is preserved. This gives students a route for checking their own calculations.

slides.title: The Extended Plane Is The Natural Domain
slides.notes: The extended plane prevents a pole from being treated as a failure of the formula. Under stereographic projection, ordinary complex numbers occupy the sphere minus the north pole, and the missing north pole records infinity. Once this picture is in place, Mobius transformations become bijections of a compact surface.

slides.title: Definition: Fractional-Linear Action
slides.notes: The matrix viewpoint is more than a notation shortcut. It explains why scalar multiples represent the same transformation and why inverse matrices produce inverse maps. The determinant condition ensures that the two rows describe independent projective data, so the map does not crush the whole plane to one value.

slides.title: Four Moves Generate The Intuition
slides.notes: The appendix can be read through a small set of elementary motions. Translations and complex multiplications feel familiar from Euclidean geometry, while the reciprocal map contributes the genuinely projective behavior. A general Mobius map is best understood by watching these actions combine rather than by staring only at four coefficients.

slides.title: Generalized Circles: Lines And Circles Together
slides.notes: The capitalized word Circle means the union of two familiar species: ordinary circles and straight lines. The real quadratic equation is the bookkeeping device that makes this union algebraically stable. Students should notice that the classification depends on a coefficient, not on drawing style.

slides.title: Mobius Maps Preserve The Circle Class
slides.notes: This slide is the geometric center of the appendix. Instead of memorizing many cases, students can track whether the source Circle passes through the pole. The notebook's numerical residuals reinforce the theorem by showing that fitted image curves obey the same generalized equation to numerical precision.

slides.title: Inversion Is Conjugate-Mobius Geometry
slides.notes: Inversion is a metric construction and a fractional-linear construction with conjugation inserted. The distance-product identity is the easiest way to test individual points, while orthogonal Circles give the global geometric invariant. This is where angle preservation separates from orientation preservation.

slides.title: The Cross-Ratio Is The Four-Point Fingerprint
slides.notes: The cross-ratio is the algebraic invariant that makes the visual Circle-preservation story feel projective. It uses four points because three distinct points can be sent to three chosen targets by a Mobius transformation. The fourth point then records meaningful data that cannot be normalized away.

slides.title: Three Points Determine The Coordinate Change
slides.notes: The three-point control principle explains why Mobius transformations are rigid despite having a flexible formula. Once three distinct source points and three distinct targets are fixed, the transformation has no remaining freedom. The cross-ratio turns this principle into an actual construction.

slides.title: Holomorphic Mobius Maps Preserve Oriented Angles
slides.notes: At a finite point away from the pole, a holomorphic Mobius map has a nonzero complex derivative. Multiplication by that derivative rotates and scales every tangent vector by the same amount. Therefore the angle between two tangent directions, including its orientation, is preserved.

slides.title: Conjugate-Mobius Maps Reverse Orientation
slides.notes: Conjugation is the simplest way to see the difference between conformal and orientation-preserving. It keeps angle sizes intact because reflection is an isometry of the plane, but it reverses the order of a local frame. The notebook visual checks this with a tiny triangle whose signed area changes sign.

slides.title: Decomposition: Reflections And Inversions
slides.notes: The final proposition in the source span points toward a structural view: these transformations can be decomposed into elementary geometric operations. That statement is useful pedagogically because inversions and reflections are easier to see than an arbitrary coefficient quadruple. It also explains why Circle preservation and angle behavior survive composition.

slides.title: Link To The Poincare Disk
slides.notes: This appendix is not isolated from the hyperbolic chapter. Disk-preserving Mobius transformations are precisely the coordinate changes that move points around the Poincare disk while preserving its geometry. The same algebra that sends Circles to Circles now sends boundary-orthogonal arcs to boundary-orthogonal arcs.

slides.title: Applied Lab: Classify Images Of Circles
slides.notes: The lab turns the preservation theorem into a diagnostic procedure. Students first make a qualitative prediction using the pole-through-Circle rule, then check it by fitting the transformed samples to the generalized-Circle equation. This is a good place to emphasize that numerical experiments are most valuable when they are tied to a theorem.

slides.title: Mobius Maps Are The Coordinate Geometry Of C_infinity
slides.notes: Close by asking students to hold two views at once. Algebraically, Mobius transformations are matrix actions on homogeneous coordinates; geometrically, they are Circle-preserving conformal transformations of the extended plane. The appendix matters because it supplies a compact language for stereographic projection, inversions, and hyperbolic disk symmetries.
